hook: The farm boy who found the rules that move the planets.

pages.x: Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day 1642 by the old calendar, at Woolsthorpe Manor, a farmhouse in Lincolnshire, three months after his father died. He was so tiny his mother said he would have fitted in a quart pot. Left with his grandmother, he grew into a lonely boy who built sundials, water clocks and a model windmill driven by a mouse on a treadmill.

pages.t: The plague years and the apple
pages.x: In 1665 plague closed Cambridge University, and Newton went home to the farm. In about eighteen months alone he worked out calculus, the secret of colour and the start of his theory of gravity. Years later he told a friend that watching an apple fall in the garden made him wonder if the same pull reached all the way to the Moon. It never hit him on the head.

To describe things that change smoothly, like the speed of a falling stone, Newton invented his 'method of fluxions', which we call calculus. The German Gottfried Leibniz found it on his own, and the two fought for years over who came first.
pages.fx: Calculus is the language of physics and engineering. Orbits, bridges, electric circuits, weather forecasts and the graphics in every video game are all worked out with it.

pages.x: With a prism in a dark room, he split a sunbeam into a band of colours, then used a second prism to put them back together into white. Lenses blurred images with coloured fringes, so in 1668 he built a telescope that used a curved mirror instead.
pages.fx: Mirror telescopes like his are the giants of astronomy today, from the great telescopes on Hawaiian mountains to the James Webb Space Telescope.

pages.x: In 1687, pushed and paid for by the astronomer Edmond Halley, Newton published the Principia. Its three laws of motion and its law of universal gravitation explained with one set of rules why apples fall, why the Moon circles the Earth, why the tides rise and when comets come back. Many call it the most important science book ever written.

In 1696 Newton left Cambridge to run the Royal Mint in London. He hunted forgers himself, in disguise in taverns, and sent the master counterfeiter William Chaloner to the gallows. Yet even Newton lost a fortune in the South Sea Bubble of 1720, and is said to have sighed that he could work out the motions of the stars but not the madness of people.

He led the Royal Society from 1703 and was knighted in 1705. He never married, feuded bitterly with rivals such as Robert Hooke and Leibniz, and spent years on alchemy and Bible prophecy. When he died in 1727 he was buried in Westminster Abbey with honours fit for a king; Voltaire, who watched, marvelled that a country could honour a scientist like that.

Newton showed that the universe runs on laws simple enough to write down and test, the same on Earth as in the heavens. Engineers still use his mechanics to launch rockets and build bridges, and Einstein began where Newton left off.
pts: Laws of motion and universal gravitation
Invented calculus, at the same time as Leibniz
Explained colour and built the mirror telescope
